About 120 million years ago, India broke away. It drifted north on a [[plate|tectonic plate]], faster than almost any other land on Earth.
Around 50 million years ago it crashed into Asia. It's still pushing north today.

sec.t:
Earth's outer shell is broken into [[plate|plates]] that move a few centimetres a year, carried by the slowly churning [[mantle|mantle]] below. Over millions of years, that adds up to thousands of kilometres.

In 1912, a German scientist named [[@continental-drift|Alfred Wegener]] suggested that the continents had once been joined and had drifted apart. He pointed to coastlines that fit together like a jigsaw, and to the same [[fossil|fossil]] plants and animals on continents now separated by oceans. A fern-like plant called Glossopteris, for example, is found in India, Africa, Australia, South America and [[@antarctica|Antarctica]].

Most scientists rejected his idea for decades, because nobody could explain what force moved the continents. Wegener died on an [[expedition|expedition]] in Greenland in 1930. Only in the 1960s did new evidence from the [[@ocean-floor-maps|ocean floor]] show he had been right.

About 66 million years ago, India passed over a hot spot in Earth's mantle, the same one that now sits under the island of Réunion. Huge cracks opened, and [[lava|lava]] poured out again and again, layer upon layer. The flows covered much of western and central India and built the [[@deccan|Deccan]] plateau. The eruptions happened around the same time as [[@extinction|the asteroid]] strike that ended the [[@dino-age-span|age of dinosaurs]]. Some scientists think the gases from the lava made things worse for life everywhere, while others think the [[asteroid|asteroid]] did almost all the damage.

You can still see those layers as giant steps in the hills of the [[@western-ghats|Western Ghats]], around places like Mahabaleshwar. The [[@soil-types-india|black soil]] of the Deccan, so good for growing [[@clothes-cotton|cotton]], formed as that lava rock weathered.

Matching rocks and fossils in India, Africa, Antarctica and Australia, magnetic patterns frozen in old lava, and modern GPS measurements all tell the same story.

Living things carry the story too. The purple frog of the Western Ghats spends most of its life underground. Its closest living relatives are tiny frogs in the Seychelles, islands that broke off from India long ago. The two lines of [[@frogs-monsoon|frogs]] have been apart ever since.

India still pushes into Asia. That's why the [[@himalaya-form|Himalayas]] keep rising and why the region has [[@earthquakes|earthquakes]].

Today scientists measure the movement with satellite navigation, the same technology behind [[@gps-how|GPS]] in phones. Fixed stations across India show the land creeping north-east by about 4 to 5 cm every year. In about a million years, that adds up to around 50 km.

text: The ozone layer is a part of the [[atmosphere|atmosphere]], mostly about 15 to 35 km above the ground, that contains more ozone than anywhere else. [[ozone|Ozone]] is a kind of oxygen. Ordinary oxygen has two oxygen [[atom|atoms]] stuck together, but ozone has three.

The ozone layer absorbs most of the Sun's harmful [[ultraviolet|ultraviolet]] light, especially the kind that causes [[@sunburn-sunscreen|sunburn]] and damages living cells. Without it, life on land would be much harder. In the 1980s, scientists discovered that chemicals made by people were thinning it. The world agreed to stop using them, and the layer is now slowly healing.

st.reveal: All the ozone above you, squeezed to the pressure at ground level, would be only about as thick as two stacked coins. Spread high in the sky, that small amount is enough to block most of the Sun's harmful ultraviolet light.

sec.t:
Ozone is spread thinly through the air, mixed with much more ordinary oxygen and nitrogen. If you could gather all the ozone above your head and squeeze it to the pressure at ground level, it would make a layer only about 3 mm thick.

Yet that small amount does a big job. When [[@how-sunglasses|ultraviolet light]] from the [[@sun-what|Sun]] hits an ozone [[molecule|molecule]], the molecule absorbs the energy and breaks apart. The pieces later join up again into new ozone. So the layer keeps absorbing ultraviolet light, over and over.

Too much ultraviolet light burns [[@skin|skin]], damages eyes and harms plants and tiny sea creatures. That's why the ozone layer matters so much.

In the late 1920s, chemists invented chlorofluorocarbons, or CFCs. They were safe to handle, didn't burn and didn't react with much, so they were used in [[@refrigerator|fridges]], [[@air-conditioning|air conditioners]] and spray cans.

In 1974, two chemists in California, Mario Molina and Sherwood Rowland, warned that CFCs would drift up into the high atmosphere. There, strong sunlight would break them apart and release chlorine. A single chlorine atom can destroy thousands of ozone molecules. Many people doubted them at first.

The discovery led to quick action. In 1987, countries signed the Montreal Protocol, agreeing to cut and then stop making CFCs and similar chemicals. India joined in 1992 and, like other developing countries, had stopped making CFCs by 2010.

In 2009, the Montreal Protocol became the first [[treaty|treaty]] in the history of the [[@united-nations|United Nations]] to be ratified by every country. In 1995, Molina, Rowland and the Dutch scientist Paul Crutzen won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for their work on ozone.

CFCs last a long time in the air, often 50 to 100 years, so the damage takes decades to repair. Scientists from the UN and the World Meteorological Organization say the ozone layer is recovering. Over Antarctica, it should return to 1980 levels around 2066, and over most of the world, around 2040.

Many of the chemicals that replaced CFCs trap heat strongly, adding to [[@climate-change|climate change]]. In 2016, countries agreed to phase those down too.

sec.h: Good up high, bad down low
sec.t:
Ozone in the high sky protects us. Ozone near the ground is a different story. It forms when sunlight cooks gases from car exhausts and factories, and it is part of [[@fog-smog|smog]]. Breathing it can make coughing and asthma worse. So scientists sometimes say ozone is "good up high, bad nearby". The same gas can help or harm, depending on where it is. Ground-level ozone is one part of the wider problem of [[@air-pollution|air pollution]].

World Ozone Day is marked every year on 16 September, the day the Montreal Protocol was signed.

text: Yes. India has two kinds of wolf. The Indian wolf lives on the dry plains and plateaus of central, western and southern India. The Himalayan wolf lives high in the mountains of [[@ladakh|Ladakh]], Himachal Pradesh and Sikkim.

Both are rare. A 2022 study estimated about 3,100 Indian wolves, roughly as many as there are wild tigers in India. Himalayan wolves number perhaps a few hundred in India. Yet wolves get far less attention than tigers, partly because they live in places most people overlook: dusty [[@grasslands|grasslands]], thorny scrub and farmers' fields.

sec.t:
The Indian wolf is much smaller than the big grey wolves of Canada or Russia. An adult weighs about 20 to 25 kilograms, about the same as a large village dog. It has a short, sandy coat that keeps it cool in the heat and blends with dry grass.

Packs are small, often a breeding pair and their young, sometimes up to eight or so. They hunt [[@wild-blackbuck|blackbuck]] and chinkara, two kinds of fast Indian antelope, as well as hares and rodents. They also take sheep and goats, which brings them into conflict with herders. They often hunt in the cool hours of dawn and dusk, and spend the hot day resting in dens, ravines or tall grass.

The most famous wolves in India are fictional. In Rudyard Kipling's [[@jungle-book|The Jungle Book]], written in the 1890s, the boy Mowgli is raised by a wolf pack in the Seeonee hills, based on the real Seoni district of Madhya Pradesh. Mother Wolf, Father Wolf and the pack leader Akela are kinder than most real wolves would be to a human child.

In villages, wolves have a mixed reputation. Herders lose animals to them. Attacks on people are very rare, but they do happen, usually where wolves have lost their natural prey. In 2024, a series of attacks near Bahraich in Uttar Pradesh frightened villagers, and forest officials spent weeks tracking and catching several wolves.

The biggest threat to Indian wolves is the loss of their home. For a long time, government maps marked open grasslands as "wasteland", land that seemed empty and useless. Much of it has been ploughed, planted with trees, built on or covered in solar farms.

A few protected places help. Velavadar Blackbuck National Park in Gujarat is famous for its wolves and blackbuck. The Deccan grasslands near Solapur in Maharashtra and parts of Rajasthan and Karnataka also hold packs. Wolves are protected under India's wildlife law, and killing them is a crime.

In the United States, wolves were wiped out from most states in the early 1900s. In 1995, they were brought back to [[@yellowstone-wolves|Yellowstone]] National Park, and scientists watched the whole [[ecosystem|ecosystem]] change, from elk herds to riverbank trees.

India's wolves never disappeared completely, but they need room. Like wolves everywhere, they keep in touch with [[@animal-communication|howls]] that can carry across kilometres of open land. One recent study found that wolves living near busy villages howl less often, as if keeping their voices down.

text: It depends on the battery. Big lead batteries from cars and inverters are usually collected and melted down, and the lead goes straight into new batteries. Lithium-ion batteries, the kind in phones, laptops and [[@electric-cars|electric cars]], can be taken apart for their valuable metals, though many are still lost.

Small batteries, like the AA cells in a remote control, often end up in household rubbish. That wastes metal, and some kinds can leak harmful chemicals into soil. Worse, lithium batteries thrown in the bin can catch fire when rubbish trucks crush them. In many countries, firefighters now see this as a growing problem.

Tiny button batteries, found in watches, car keys and toys, carry another danger. If a small child swallows one, it can burn the inside of the throat within about two hours. Doctors say anyone who sees a child swallow one should get medical help straight away. That's one more reason to keep old batteries in a closed box, out of reach.

sec.t:
Inside a phone or car battery are thin sheets coated with lithium, cobalt, nickel, manganese and copper. These metals are mined in only a few places and are expensive, so there is money in getting them back.

First the batteries are fully discharged, so they can't spark. Then machines shred them. The plastic and metal casings are sorted out, leaving a dark powder that recyclers call black mass. Chemicals [[dissolve|dissolve]] the black mass, and each metal is pulled out separately to be made into new [[@batteries|batteries]]. Some plants use furnaces instead, melting everything and separating the metals afterwards. Recycling also eases pressure on mining. Much of the world's cobalt comes from the Democratic Republic of the Congo, where some mines have been found using child labour.

Electric car batteries slowly hold less charge. After about ten years, a car's battery may only hold 70 to 80 percent of what it once did. That might be too little for long drives, but it is plenty for sitting still.

So some old car batteries get a second job. Companies link them together to store electricity from [[@solar-panels|solar panels]] during the day and release it at night. Only when they are completely worn out do they go for recycling.

In 2022, India brought in rules saying that companies selling batteries must also collect and recycle a share of them. The USA, the European Union and other places have similar laws, and Europe now asks new batteries to contain some recycled metal.

Rules only work if old batteries reach the right place, though. Most of them still sit in drawers, mixed with other [[@e-waste|e-waste]] such as old phones and chargers. Many shops and municipal collection points take used batteries. The safest home habit is a box kept away from heat, and a trip to drop them off when it fills up.

text: A video is really a stack of still pictures, called frames, shown quickly one after another. Normal video records about 24 to 30 frames every second. Your eyes and brain blend them together into smooth movement, the trick explained in [[@movies-move|how movies move]].

A slow-motion camera takes many more frames every second, such as 240, 1,000 or even millions. Then it plays them back at normal speed. If a camera records 240 frames in one second and plays them at 30 a second, that single second stretches out to 8 seconds on screen. Nothing is slowed down. The camera has simply captured far more moments.

st.reveal: 240 divided by 30 is 8. Every real second of action becomes 8 seconds on screen. That is why a one-second splash in a puddle turns into a long, beautiful ripple.

sec.t:
In the 1930s, the American engineer Harold Edgerton at MIT used flashes of light lasting a tiny fraction of a second to freeze movement. His photographs showed a bullet bursting through an apple and, in 1957, a drop of milk splashing into a perfect crown of tiny droplets.

That "Milk Drop Coronet" photo is now in museums. It showed people a hidden world that had always been there, just too quick to see. Edgerton's flash inventions later helped photograph nuclear tests and the deep sea.

sec.h: Why it needs so much light
sec.t:
Every frame needs light to make a picture. At 30 frames a second, each frame can collect light for up to a thirtieth of a second. At 1,000 frames a second, each gets a thousandth or less. Less light means darker, grainier pictures.

That is why slow motion looks best outdoors in sunshine or under bright studio lamps. It also explains a strange effect: many lights, including LED bulbs, flicker on and off very fast. Your eyes can't notice, but a slow-motion camera often can, and the room seems to pulse.

Scientists use high-speed cameras to study things too fast for eyes. They film [[@hummingbirds|hummingbird]] wings beating about 50 times a second, insects taking off, car crash tests and the moment a lightning bolt branches across the sky. Engineers check how engines spin and how phones survive being dropped.

Some research cameras reach millions of frames a second. In 2011, a team at MIT led by Ramesh Raskar, an engineer who grew up in Nashik, went much further. Using a laser and a special technique that combines many repeated shots, they captured light itself moving through a plastic bottle, at a rate equivalent to about a trillion frames a second.

High-speed cameras once cost as much as a car. Now many phones film at 240 frames a second, and some have tried 960 for very short clips. Cricket broadcasters use slow-motion replays to check whether the ball hit the bat, and football referees use them to judge offside.

Sports science teams film athletes to study every step of a sprint or a bowling action. And the smartphone camera in your hand is the result of decades of shrinking lenses and [[sensor|sensors]], the story of [[@cameras-phones|phone cameras]].

text: Hip-hop began in the Bronx, a part of New York City, in the early 1970s. Young people, mostly African American and Latino, held parties in community rooms, parks and streets. DJs played funk and soul records, and dancers waited for the "break", the short section where the singing stopped and only the drums kept going.

A teenage DJ called Kool Herc started using two turntables to repeat the break over and over. Soon, other performers began talking in rhyme over these beats to hype up the crowd. That rhyming became rap. Dancing, art and [[@fashion-history|fashion]] grew alongside, and together they formed hip-hop.

st.reveal: Dancers loved the "break", the part of a song where the singing stopped and only drums played. Using two turntables and two copies of a record, Herc could jump from one to the other and stretch a few seconds of drums into minutes.

myth: Hip-hop and rap are just two names for the same thing.
Rap is one part of hip-hop. Hip-hop is a whole culture that also includes DJing, breaking (a style of dance) and graffiti art, along with its own fashion and language.

sec.h: A tough time in the Bronx
sec.t:
In the 1970s, many neighbourhoods of the South Bronx were struggling. A huge highway had cut through communities, many families had little money, and fires destroyed thousands of buildings. Clubs were expensive, and young people had few places to go.

So they made their own fun. With borrowed speakers, records and a lot of creativity, they turned schoolyards and apartment-block rooms into dance floors. Hip-hop was born from people making something exciting out of very little, in one of the most famous cities on Earth, [[@new-york|New York]].

Hip-hop is often described as having four [[element|elements]]. DJing is creating beats from records. MCing, or rapping, is rhyming over the beat. Breaking is an athletic dance with spins, freezes and footwork, done by b-boys and b-girls.

The fourth element is graffiti, bold painted words and images, often on trains and walls. Painting on property without permission is against the law, but many graffiti artists now create large [[mural|murals]] with permission.

sec.h: From the Bronx to the world
sec.t:
In 1979, a song called *Rapper's Delight* by the Sugarhill Gang became a hit, and many people heard rap for the first time. Over the next decades, hip-hop became one of the most popular kinds of music in the USA.

Rappers have been praised as poets. In 2018, the rapper Kendrick Lamar won a Pulitzer Prize for Music, the first winner from outside classical music and jazz. Like [[@poetry|poetry]], good rap depends on [[rhythm|rhythm]], rhyme and clever wordplay. Breaking made its debut as a medal sport at the 2024 Paris [[@olympics|Olympics]].

Hip-hop reached India through music videos, films and the [[@internet-how|internet]]. In the 2010s, young rappers in [[@mumbai|Mumbai]], some from neighbourhoods like [[@slums-housing|Dharavi]], began rapping in Hindi and other Indian languages about their own streets and lives.

The 2019 Hindi film *Gully Boy* was inspired by the stories of real Mumbai rappers. Today, Indian rap is sung in Punjabi, Tamil, [[@malayalam|Malayalam]], Marathi and many other languages. B-boys and b-girls practise breaking in cities from Delhi to [[@bengaluru|Bengaluru]], and some now compete internationally.

text: भारतीय गहनों की परंपरा दुनिया की सबसे पुरानी परंपराओं में से एक है। यहाँ के लोग हज़ारों सालों से चूड़ियाँ, हार, झुमके और नथ पहनते आए हैं। ये सोने, चाँदी, शंख, काँच, मनकों, फूलों, और लाख से भी बनते रहे हैं। लाख एक तरह की राल है जिसे कीड़े बनाते हैं।

भारत में गहने सिर्फ़ सजने-सँवरने की चीज़ नहीं हैं। उनसे पता चल सकता है कि कोई किस इलाके का है, कोई स्त्री शादीशुदा है या नहीं, या परिवार किस धर्म को मानता है। शादी, जन्म और त्योहार, सब गहनों के साथ मनाए जाते हैं। बहुत-से परिवारों के लिए यह बचत का भी एक तरीका है, क्योंकि सोने की कीमत बनी रहती है। हर इलाके की अपनी शैली है, राजस्थान के नगों से जड़े कुंदन से लेकर तमिलनाडु के सोने के मंदिर-गहनों तक।

sec.t:
प्राचीन [[@indus-cities|सिंधु घाटी के शहरों]] में लोग शंख, ताँबे और पकी मिट्टी की चूड़ियाँ बनाते थे, और कार्नेलियन नाम के लाल-नारंगी पत्थर के मनके। कार्नेलियन के कुछ मनकों में पूरी लंबाई के आर-पार बारीक छेद किए गए थे, जो बहुत धीरज और हुनर का काम था। हड़प्पा के मनके दूर मेसोपोटामिया तक मिले हैं, जो आज के इराक में है।

मोहनजोदड़ो की काँसे की मशहूर 'नाचती लड़की' आज दिल्ली के राष्ट्रीय संग्रहालय में है। उसकी लगभग पूरी बाईं बाँह चूड़ियों से ढकी है। भारत में आज भी बहुत-सी महिलाएँ चूड़ियाँ पहनती हैं, अक्सर काँच की, जो हाथ हिलाते ही खनकती हैं।

**कुंदन** राजस्थान और मुग़ल दरबारों से आया। कारीगर बिना कटे या सपाट कटे नगों को बहुत शुद्ध सोने की पन्नी की परत में दबाकर बिठाते हैं। यह पन्नी ही नगों को थामे रखती है, किसी पंजे या खाँचे की ज़रूरत नहीं पड़ती। कुंदन गहने का पिछला हिस्सा अक्सर **मीनाकारी** से सजा होता है। इसमें लाल, हरे और नीले चटख [[enamel|मीने]] के रंग आँच से धातु पर पक्के कर दिए जाते हैं। जयपुर दोनों के लिए मशहूर है।

तमिलनाडु के **मंदिर-गहने** नागरकोइल जैसे कस्बों में बनते हैं। पहले ये देवताओं की मूर्तियों को सजाने के लिए बनाए गए थे, बाद में भरतनाट्यम की नर्तकियाँ और दुल्हनें इन्हें पहनने लगीं। इनमें सोने में देवी-देवता, मोर और कमल बने होते हैं। ओडिशा में कटक के कारीगर **तारकशी** करते हैं। इसमें चाँदी के पतले-पतले तारों को ऐंठकर फूलों और लेस जैसे नाज़ुक डिज़ाइन बनाए जाते हैं।

sec.h: गहने और ज़िंदगी के बड़े पल
sec.t:
बहुत-सी हिंदू शादियों में दूल्हा दुल्हन के गले में मंगलसूत्र बाँधता है, जो काले मनकों और सोने का हार होता है। भारत के कई हिस्सों में शादीशुदा महिलाएँ बिछिया, लाल-सफ़ेद चूड़ियाँ या नथ भी पहनती हैं। मुस्लिम, सिख और ईसाई परिवारों की अपनी परंपराएँ हैं, सिखों के स्टील के कड़े से लेकर केरल के सीरियाई ईसाई परिवारों के शादी के हारों तक।

[[@weddings-india|शादी]] में दुल्हन को मिला सोना परंपरा से उसकी अपनी संपत्ति माना जाता रहा है, बुरे वक्त का सहारा। यह भी एक वजह है कि भारतीय परिवार इतना सोना खरीदते हैं।

पुराने ज़माने में भारत के राजा और रईस अक्सर रानियों से भी ज़्यादा गहने पहनते थे: मोतियों की लड़ियाँ, बाजूबंद और रत्नजड़ित पगड़ियाँ। कई समुदायों में पुरुष आज भी अँगूठियाँ, चेन और कान की बालियाँ पहनते हैं। दक्कन में बीदर के कारीगरों ने [[@bidri|बिदरी]] कला विकसित की, जिसमें काली धातु में चाँदी जड़ी जाती है। इससे गहनों के साथ-साथ डिब्बियाँ और हुक्के भी बनते थे। गहने का एक ही टुकड़ा किसी परिवार का पूरा इतिहास सँजोए रह सकता है, जो पीढ़ी दर पीढ़ी दादी-नानी से पोती-नातिन तक पहुँचता है।

text: लता मंगेशकर भारत की सबसे महान गायिकाओं में से एक थीं। 1940 के दशक के आखिर से करीब सात दशकों तक उन्होंने हिंदी फ़िल्मों के लिए और 30 से ज़्यादा भाषाओं में हज़ारों गाने गाए। उनकी साफ़, ऊँची, मीठी आवाज़ परदे पर अनगिनत नायिकाओं की आवाज़ बन गई।

वे पार्श्व गायिका (प्लेबैक सिंगर) थीं। यानी उनके गाने [[@behind-music-recording|स्टूडियो में रिकॉर्ड होते]] थे, और परदे पर अभिनेता उन पर होंठ हिलाते थे। लोग उन्हें 'स्वर कोकिला' और 'भारत की कोकिला' कहते थे। 2001 में उन्हें भारत रत्न मिला, जो देश का सबसे बड़ा नागरिक सम्मान है। 2022 में जब 92 साल की उम्र में उनका निधन हुआ, तो सरकार ने दो दिन के राष्ट्रीय शोक की घोषणा की।

sec.t:
लता का जन्म 1929 में इंदौर में हुआ, जो आज [[@madhya-pradesh|मध्य प्रदेश]] में है। उनके पिता दीनानाथ मंगेशकर एक जाने-माने शास्त्रीय गायक और [[@marathi-gujarati|मराठी रंगमंच]] के अभिनेता थे। उन्होंने लता को बहुत छोटी उम्र से ही संगीत सिखाना शुरू कर दिया।

1942 में, जब लता लगभग 13 साल की थीं, उनके पिता चल बसे। पाँच बच्चों में सबसे बड़ी होने के नाते परिवार का बोझ लता पर आ गया। उन्होंने मराठी फ़िल्मों में छोटी-छोटी भूमिकाएँ कीं और गाने गाए। उनकी बहनें आशा, उषा और मीना और भाई हृदयनाथ, सब आगे चलकर संगीतकार बने।

परिवार बंबई, यानी आज के [[@mumbai|मुंबई]], आ गया। लता की आवाज़ ऊँची और हल्की थी, उन दिनों फ़िल्मों में चलने वाली भारी आवाज़ों से बिल्कुल अलग। कहते हैं एक निर्माता ने उन्हें यह कहकर ठुकरा दिया कि आवाज़ बहुत पतली है।

संगीतकार ग़ुलाम हैदर को उन पर भरोसा था। फिर 1949 में उन्होंने फ़िल्म *महल* में *आएगा आनेवाला* गाया। यह दिल में उतर जाने वाला गाना ज़बरदस्त हिट हुआ, और स्टूडियो उन्हें बुलाने लगे। 1950 और 1960 के दशक में उन्होंने हिंदी फ़िल्मों के लगभग हर बड़े [[@film-music-composers|संगीतकार]] के लिए गाया।

sec.h: वह गाना जिसने देश को रुला दिया

sec.t:
लता की आवाज़ इस बात के लिए मशहूर थी कि बहुत ऊँचे [[pitch|सुरों]] पर भी वह शुद्ध और स्थिर रहती थी। वे धीमे गाकर भी साफ़ सुनाई देती थीं, उनकी [[sound|ध्वनि]] कहीं धुँधली नहीं होती थी, जो फ़िल्मों के [[@microphones|माइक्रोफ़ोन]] के लिए बिल्कुल ठीक था। वे हिंदी और उर्दू के शब्दों का उच्चारण बड़े ध्यान से करती थीं, इसलिए हर पंक्ति आसानी से समझ आती थी। आवाज़ ऊँचे सुरों तक कैसे पहुँचती है, यह [[@singing|गायन]] में पढ़ो।

वे रोज़ रियाज़ करती थीं और अपनी आवाज़ का, यानी गले के [[larynx|स्वरयंत्र]] का, पूरा ख्याल रखती थीं। गायकों के साथ क्या न्याय है, इसकी भी उन्हें गहरी समझ थी। 1960 के दशक में उन्होंने आवाज़ उठाई कि रिकॉर्ड की बिक्री से होने वाली कमाई, यानी रॉयल्टी में पार्श्व गायकों का भी हिस्सा होना चाहिए। इससे कुछ संगीतकारों और साथी गायकों के साथ उनकी लंबी अनबन चली।

दशकों तक हिंदी फ़िल्मों के महिला गानों का बहुत बड़ा हिस्सा लता और उनकी बहन आशा भोसले ने गाया। कुछ आलोचकों और गायकों को लगा कि उनके दबदबे की वजह से दूसरी गायिकाओं को मौके मिलना मुश्किल हो गया। दूसरे कहते हैं कि संगीतकार बस उन्हीं की आवाज़ें चाहते थे।

वे अस्सी की उम्र पार करने के बाद भी गाती रहीं। एस. डी. बर्मन से लेकर [[@ar-rahman|ए. आर. रहमान]] तक, सब संगीतकारों ने उनके साथ काम किया। आज सत्तर साल से भी पहले रिकॉर्ड किए उनके गाने शादियों में, रेडियो पर और स्ट्रीमिंग ऐप्स पर पूरी दुनिया में बजते हैं।

text: Nandalal Bose (1882–1966) was one of India's most important modern artists and art teachers. A student of Abanindranath Tagore in the [[@bengal-school|Bengal School]], he went on to lead Kala Bhavana, the art school at Santiniketan, for decades.

He painted gods and epics, village life and nature. He made posters for the freedom movement at Gandhi's request. And he and his students decorated the pages of the original Constitution of India. For him, art wasn't only for galleries. It belonged in homes, walls, festivals and daily life.

sec.t:
Nandalal was born in 1882 in Bihar and studied in Kolkata, where he joined Abanindranath Tagore's classes in 1905. He learned to paint in the soft, Indian-inspired style of the Bengal School.

He also loved the folk arts of Bengal: the painted scrolls of storytellers, clay dolls and the patterns women drew on floors for festivals. He believed these were as much a part of Indian art as temple [[sculpture|sculpture]].

In 1909, he travelled to the Ajanta caves with an English artist, Christiana Herringham, to copy the ancient [[mural|murals]]. Sitting for weeks in the dim caves, studying paintings more than 1,500 years old, changed how he saw line and colour. Later he studied the [[fresco|frescoes]] at Bagh, in Madhya Pradesh, too. These visits gave his work its strong, flowing outlines.

In 1921, [[@tagore|Rabindranath Tagore]] founded Visva-Bharati at Santiniketan, a university where classes were often held outdoors under trees. Nandalal joined its art school, Kala Bhavana, and soon became its head.

He taught students to draw from nature, to watch birds, trees and people closely, and to try many crafts: murals, woodcuts, [[textile|textiles]], pottery and festival decorations. He travelled with Tagore to China and Japan in 1924. His students included K. G. Subramanyan, Ramkinkar Baij and Benode Behari Mukherjee, who became great artists themselves.

When India's [[@constitution|Constitution]] was ready, it was written out by hand in beautiful [[calligraphy|calligraphy]]. Nandalal Bose and his students were asked to decorate it. They painted borders and pictures for each part, telling India's long story. There is a seal from Mohenjo-daro, scenes from the Ramayana and Mahabharata, the Buddha and Emperor Ashoka. Later pages show Akbar's court, Shivaji, Gandhi's Dandi March and more.

One of his students, Beohar Rammanohar Sinha, painted several pages, including the decorated border around the Preamble. The original volumes are kept in special sealed cases in the library of Parliament in New Delhi.

After independence, Nandalal Bose designed the emblems for the Bharat Ratna and the Padma Shri awards. He received the Padma Vibhushan in 1954. The Government of India later declared his works "national art treasures", meaning they cannot be taken out of the country.

He died at Santiniketan in 1966. Many of his paintings are at the National Gallery of Modern Art in New Delhi. His students carried his habits all over India: drawing outdoors, respecting village crafts, and treating a festival decoration as seriously as a painting in a frame.

sec.t:
जमैका 1962 में ब्रिटेन से आज़ाद हुआ। उन्हीं सालों में जमैका के नौजवान संगीतकारों ने अमेरिकी रिदम एंड ब्लूज़ को द्वीप के अपने लोक संगीत, मेंटो, के साथ मिलाकर स्का बनाया। यह तेज़ था, इसमें बिगुल जैसे साज़ थे और उछलती ऑफ़-बीट।

1960 के दशक के बीच में यह संगीत धीमा होकर रॉकस्टेडी बन गया, ज़्यादा ठंडा-ठंडा और बेस पर भारी। लगभग 1968 तक यह और धीमा हुआ, बदला, और रेगे बन गया। टूट्स एंड द मेटल्स का गाना "डू द रेगे" यह नाम इस्तेमाल करने वाले पहले गानों में से था। यह शब्द कहाँ से आया, कोई पक्के तौर पर नहीं जानता।

बॉब मार्ली किंग्स्टन के एक मोहल्ले ट्रेंच टाउन में ग़रीबी में पले-बढ़े। द वेलर्स के साथ उन्होंने "वन लव", "थ्री लिटिल बर्ड्स", "गेट अप, स्टैंड अप" और "रिडेम्पशन सॉन्ग" जैसे गाने लिखे। उनके संगीत में [[@behind-theme-music|ज़ुबान पर चढ़ जाने वाली धुनें]] भी थीं और आज़ादी, बराबरी और उम्मीद के संदेश भी।

मार्ली ने पूरी दुनिया के दौरे किए, और 1980 में ज़िम्बाब्वे की आज़ादी के जश्न में गाया। 1981 में 36 साल की उम्र में कैंसर से उनकी मृत्यु हो गई। उनकी मृत्यु के बाद आया उनका एल्बम *लेजेंड* अब तक के सबसे ज़्यादा बिकने वाले एल्बमों में से है।

बहुत से रेगे संगीतकार रस्ताफ़री को मानते हैं, जो 1930 के दशक में जमैका में शुरू हुई एक आस्था है। रस्ताफ़री अफ़्रीकी विरासत पर गर्व सिखाती है और [[@ethiopia|इथियोपिया]] के [[emperor|सम्राट]] रहे हाइले सेलासी को एक पवित्र व्यक्ति मानती है। इसीलिए इथियोपिया के झंडे के लाल, सुनहरे और हरे रंग रेगे के पोस्टरों और कपड़ों पर इतने दिखते हैं। हर रेगे कलाकार रस्ताफ़री नहीं है, और इस संगीत के संदेश भी कई तरह के हैं।

जमैका के लोगों की जड़ें कई जगह हैं। ज़्यादातर जमैकावासी उन अफ़्रीकियों के [[descendant|वंशज]] हैं जिन्हें [[@slavery-freedom|ग़ुलाम]] बनाकर इस द्वीप पर लाया गया था। 1845 से भारत से भी हज़ारों मज़दूर बागानों में काम करने वहाँ पहुँचे, और भारतीय मूल के जमैकावासी आज भी द्वीप के मेल-जोल का हिस्सा हैं। जमैका की करी गोट, यानी बकरे की करी, उन्हीं की देन है।

रेगे हर जगह पहुँच गया है। जापान, ब्राज़ील, [[@nigeria|नाइजीरिया]] और ब्रिटेन में रेगे बैंड हैं। भारत में रेगे और डब बैंड क्लबों और [[@festivals-music|संगीत समारोहों]] में बजाते हैं, और देश भर के कॉलेज कैंपसों में बॉब मार्ली के गाने जाने-पहचाने हैं।

text: रॉक एंड रोल 1950 के दशक की शुरुआत से बीच तक अमेरिका में परवान चढ़ा। इसमें अश्वेत अमेरिकियों का डांस संगीत, रिदम एंड ब्लूज़, गॉस्पेल और [[@country-music|कंट्री संगीत]] के साथ घुल-मिल गया। नतीजा था एक ऊँचे [[decibel|डेसिबल]] वाला, तेज़ और नाचने के लिए बना संगीत, धमाधम [[rhythm|ताल]] और इलेक्ट्रिक गिटार की [[vibration|झनझनाहट]] के साथ।

किशोरों को यह बहुत भाया। पहली बार नौजवानों के पास रिकॉर्ड और रेडियो पर ख़र्च करने को पैसे थे, और वे अपना ख़ुद का संगीत चाहते थे। कुछ ही सालों में चक बेरी, लिटिल रिचर्ड और एल्विस प्रेस्ली जैसे सितारों ने रॉक एंड रोल को देश की सबसे रोमांचक आवाज़ बना दिया, और जल्दी ही दुनिया के बड़े हिस्से की भी।

रॉक एंड रोल की बहुत सी सामग्री 1940 के दशक में पहले से मौजूद थी। रिदम एंड ब्लूज़ बैंड भोंपू जैसे सैक्सोफ़ोन के साथ ज़ोरदार डांस संगीत बजाते थे। अश्वेत गिरजाघरों में गॉस्पेल गायक ज़बरदस्त जोश से गाते थे।

अर्कांसस की गॉस्पेल गायिका सिस्टर रोज़ेटा थार्प 1930 और 1940 के दशक में ऐसी शैली और दमख़म से इलेक्ट्रिक गिटार बजाती थीं कि लोग दंग रह जाते थे। बाद के सितारों ने उन्हें अपनी प्रेरणा बताया। 1951 में *रॉकेट 88* नाम का एक रिकॉर्ड हिट हुआ, जिसमें गिटार की आवाज़ भर्राई और फटी-फटी सी थी। कुछ लोग इसे पहला रॉक एंड रोल रिकॉर्ड कहते हैं, हालाँकि दूसरे लोग दूसरे गाने चुनते हैं।

1950 के दशक में अमेरिका के बड़े हिस्से में नस्लीय अलगाव था: अश्वेत और श्वेत अमेरिकियों को क़ानून और रिवाज से अलग-अलग रखा जाता था, जैसा तुम [[@civil-rights|नागरिक अधिकार]] में पढ़ सकते हो। रेडियो स्टेशन और रिकॉर्ड की दुकानें भी अक्सर संगीत को "अश्वेत" और "श्वेत" में बाँट देती थीं।

रॉक एंड रोल ने ये हदें पार कर दीं। श्वेत किशोर अश्वेत कलाकारों को सुनते थे, और कुछ कॉन्सर्टों में मिली-जुली भीड़ होती थी, जिससे कुछ बड़े नाराज़ होते थे। पर यह सबके लिए बराबरी वाला नहीं था। अश्वेत संगीतकार अक्सर उन श्वेत गायकों से बहुत कम कमाते थे जो उन्हीं के गानों के "कवर" रूप रिकॉर्ड करते थे, और बहुतों को कभी पूरा श्रेय नहीं मिला। इतिहासकार आज भी इसे रॉक एंड रोल की कहानी का हिस्सा मानते हैं।

टेनेसी के मेम्फ़िस का नौजवान गायक एल्विस प्रेस्ली सबसे बड़ा सितारा बना। 1954 में सन रिकॉर्ड्स नाम के एक छोटे स्टूडियो में बने उनके पहले रिकॉर्डों में ब्लूज़ और कंट्री का मेल था। [[@television-invented|टेलीविज़न]] पर कूल्हे मटकाते उनके डांस से कुछ माँ-बाप चौंक गए और उनके बच्चे झूम उठे।

बहुत से बड़ों को लगता था कि रॉक एंड रोल शोर-शराबा है और बच्चों को बिगाड़ता है। कुछ रेडियो स्टेशनों ने इसे बजाने से मना कर दिया। इससे किशोरों को यह और भी ज़्यादा पसंद आने लगा।

1960 के दशक में [[@beatles-music|बीटल्स]] और रोलिंग स्टोन्स जैसे ब्रिटिश बैंडों ने रॉक एंड रोल लिया, उसमें अपने विचार जोड़े और उसे अटलांटिक पार वापस अमेरिका भेज दिया। 1965 में बीटल्स के जॉर्ज हैरिसन ने बीटल्स के एक गाने में सितार बजाया। बाद में उन्होंने भारतीय सितार वादक [[@ravi-shankar|रवि शंकर]] से सीखा।

1968 में बीटल्स ने [[@uttarakhand|ऋषिकेश]] के एक आश्रम में हफ़्तों बिताए, [[@mindfulness|ध्यान]] सीखा और गाने लिखे, जैसा तुम [[@beatles-india|भारत में बीटल्स]] में पढ़ सकते हो। आगे चलकर रॉक हेवी मेटल से लेकर पंक तक कई शैलियों में बँट गया। भारत का भी अपना रॉक संसार है, जहाँ बैंड अंग्रेज़ी, हिंदी और कई दूसरी भारतीय भाषाओं में गाते हैं।

text: स्टैच्यू ऑफ़ लिबर्टी पर ताँबा चढ़ा है, वही लाल-भूरी धातु जो बिजली के तारों में होती है। जब ताँबा सालों तक हवा और बारिश में रहता है, तो वह धीरे-धीरे पानी, [[oxygen|ऑक्सीजन]] और दूसरी गैसों से क्रिया करता है। उसके ऊपर एक पतली हरी पपड़ी जम जाती है, जिसे [[patina|पैटिना]] कहते हैं।

यह मूर्ति न्यूयॉर्क पहुँची तो नए सिक्के की तरह चमकीली और भूरी थी, और 1886 में इसे समर्पित किया गया। कुछ ही दशकों में यह पूरी तरह हरी हो गई। आज तस्वीरों में जो रंग दिखता है, वह रसायन और मौसम का कमाल है, रंग-रोगन का नहीं।

sec.t:
पैटिना कोई नुकसान नहीं है। जिन वैज्ञानिकों ने इसका अध्ययन किया, उन्होंने पाया कि यह ज़्यादातर ऐसे [[mineral|खनिजों]] से बनी है जिनमें ताँबा, गंधक और ऑक्सीजन हैं। यह कुछ हद तक एक बड़े शहर की प्रदूषित हवा में मौजूद गंधक से बनी। यह धातु से कसकर चिपकी रहती है और आगे के बदलाव को धीमा कर देती है, कुछ-कुछ बरसाती की तरह।

[[@mystery-iron-pillar|लोहे का बर्ताव अलग है]]। जब लोहे पर [[@rust|जंग]] लगती है, तो परतदार जंग झड़कर गिर जाती है और नीचे की नई धातु खुल जाती है, इसलिए जंग और गहरे तक खाती जाती है। ताँबे का हरा कोट अपनी जगह टिका रहता है। 1900 के दशक की शुरुआत में जब अमेरिकी सरकार ने मूर्ति को रंगने पर विचार किया, तो [[@newspapers|अख़बारों]] और आम लोगों ने एतराज़ किया। हरा रंग बना रहा, और अब यह दुनिया भर में लोगों के मन में बसी इस मूर्ति की तस्वीर का हिस्सा है।

अंदर लोग चबूतरे के ऊपर से मुकुट तक 162 सीढ़ियों वाली एक तंग घुमावदार सीढ़ी चढ़ सकते हैं। मुकुट में 25 खिड़कियाँ हैं। मशाल 1916 से आम लोगों के लिए बंद है, जब पास के एक युद्धकालीन गोला-बारूद भंडार में धमाके से बाँह को नुकसान पहुँचा था।

मूर्ति का ख़र्च फ़्रांस ने उठाया, पर चबूतरे, यानी पत्थर के ऊँचे आधार, का पैसा अमेरिकियों को देना था। पैसा कम पड़ गया। 1885 में अख़बार मालिक जोसेफ़ पुलित्ज़र ने वादा किया कि वे अपने अख़बार *न्यूयॉर्क वर्ल्ड* में हर दानदाता का नाम छापेंगे, चाहे दान कितना भी छोटा हो। 1,20,000 से ज़्यादा लोगों ने पैसे दिए, जिनमें से बहुतों ने एक डॉलर से भी कम, और चबूतरा पूरा हो गया।

1903 में चबूतरे के अंदर एम्मा लाज़रस की कविता "द न्यू कोलोसस" वाली एक तख़्ती लगाई गई। "एक-दूसरे से सटी भीड़" का स्वागत करने वाली इसकी पंक्तियों ने इस मूर्ति को उन लाखों [[@immigration-stories|प्रवासियों]] से जोड़ दिया जो पास के [[@ellis-island|एलिस आइलैंड]] जाते हुए इसके पास से गुज़रे।

कलाकार बहुत पहले से जान-बूझकर ताँबे के रंग इस्तेमाल करते आए हैं। मैलाकाइट जैसे ताँबे वाले खनिजों से पुराने चित्रकारों को गहरा हरा रंग मिला, और एज़ुराइट से नीला। [[@ajanta-colours|अजंता]] के चित्रकार भी कुछ इसी तरह धरती से खनिज पीसकर अपने रंग बनाते थे।

दुनिया भर में पुराने गिरजाघरों और सरकारी इमारतों की ताँबे की छतें भी हरी हो जाती हैं। मूर्ति पर यह बदलाव दशकों में हुआ। ताँबे की सस्ती अँगूठी यह कहीं जल्दी कर सकती है। कुछ ही दिनों में वह उँगली पर हल्का हरा निशान छोड़ देती है: तुम्हारा अपना नन्हा-सा पैटिना।

text: Zaha Hadid was an Iraqi-British architect, born in Baghdad in 1950. She became famous for buildings full of sweeping curves and sharp angles, which seem to flow and twist instead of standing still. People called her the "Queen of the Curve".

In 2004, she became the first woman to win the Pritzker Prize, the top award in [[architecture|architecture]]. In 2016, she became the first woman to receive the Royal Gold Medal of the Royal Institute of British Architects on her own. She died suddenly later that year, at 65, but her firm in [[@london|London]] still designs buildings across the world.

sec.t:
Hadid grew up in Baghdad, an old city on the Tigris river not far from the ruins of [[@mesopotamia|Mesopotamia]], where some of the world's [[@first-cities|first cities]] were built. Her family valued education, and as a girl she went to schools in Iraq and abroad.

She first studied mathematics at the American University of Beirut in Lebanon. Then, in 1972, she moved to London to study at the Architectural Association, a famous school for bold ideas. There she was inspired by Russian artists of the early 1900s who painted floating shapes and broken lines. She began making paintings of her own buildings, with walls and floors exploding apart like pieces in a storm.

Hadid's ideas grew easier to build as [[@computers-how|computers]] improved. Her team used powerful design software to model complex curved surfaces and work out exactly how to make each part. Some programs had first been made for designing cars and aeroplanes.

Her training in maths helped too. A building with no straight walls needs careful [[geometry|geometry]] so it can stand up, keep out the rain and be built at a sensible cost. Her firm became known for working closely with engineers to find a way.

From the late 1990s, Hadid's buildings appeared on almost every continent. The MAXXI art museum in Rome opened in 2010, with long concrete galleries that cross over each other like ribbons. The Guangzhou Opera House in China opened the same year. The Heydar Aliyev Center in Baku, Azerbaijan, completed in 2012, rises from the ground like a white wave.

For the 2012 [[@olympics|Olympics]] in London, she designed the Aquatics Centre, with a curving roof shaped like a wave of water. Swimmers and divers there won Olympic medals beneath it.

Not everyone loved her work. Some critics said her buildings cost too much and paid more attention to looks than to the people using them. She was also questioned about working conditions for labourers building stadiums for the 2022 football World Cup in Qatar, where she had designed one of the venues.

Hadid was known for being fierce and demanding, and she worked in a field where few women reached the top. She once said that being a woman and an Arab made it harder to be taken seriously. Today, many young architects, especially women, name her as an inspiration.

text: A flag is a quick way to say "this belongs to us" or "we are here". A piece of coloured cloth can be seen from far away, it is easy to make, and anyone can recognise it without reading a word.

Flags began as markers on battlefields and ships, so soldiers and sailors could tell friend from enemy. Over time, countries adopted national flags to stand for the whole nation. Today a flag flies over government buildings, at sports events, on spacecraft and at the United Nations. People stand for it, cheer for it and sometimes argue about how it should be treated.

myth: In the USA, a flag that touches the ground must be burned.

The US Flag Code says the flag should not touch the ground, but it does not say a flag must be destroyed if it does. It can be cleaned and flown again. Worn-out flags are retired respectfully, often by burning in a ceremony.

sec.t:
Ancient armies carried standards, poles topped with banners or symbols, and Roman legions carried a metal eagle. Ships flew flags to signal which country they belonged to. National flags, the kind that stand for a whole people, became common only in the last few hundred years. Denmark's red flag with a white cross is often called the oldest national flag still in use, and a legend dates it to 1219.

The study of flags is called vexillology, from the Latin word for a banner.

For years, private citizens in India could fly the flag only on certain national days. Industrialist Naveen Jindal challenged this after being told to take down a flag at his factory. In 2004, the Supreme Court ruled that flying the flag with respect is part of a citizen's freedom of expression. The Flag Code of India, 2002, now lets people fly it on any day, as long as they treat it with dignity.

The US flag has 13 red and white stripes for the original 13 colonies and [[@usa-statehood|50 white stars]] on a blue square, one for each state. A star is added whenever a state joins, so the flag has changed 27 times. The current version has flown since 1960. The US celebrates Flag Day each year on 14 June.

In 1969, the [[@moon-landing-sites|Apollo 11]] astronauts planted a US flag on the [[@apollo-moon|Moon]]. Because there is no air there, a metal rod along the top held it out so it looked like it was waving. Flags have also been carried to the top of [[@everest-first|Mount Everest]] and painted on spacecraft, including India's lunar landers.

Most flags use only a few colours, and many are symmetrical, the same on the left as on the right. That makes them easy to sew, easy to see and easy to draw. If you look through the [[@flags-world|flags of the world]], you will find red is one of the most common colours, and stripes and crosses appear again and again.

text: To work out how long a journey takes, divide the distance by the speed. If a train goes 300 km at an average of 100 km/h, it takes 300 ÷ 100 = 3 hours.

The same rule can be turned around. Speed is distance divided by time, and distance is speed multiplied by time. Some people remember it with a triangle: D at the top, S and T at the bottom. Cover the one you want, and the other two show you what to do.
The tricky parts are not the division. They are using the right units, turning [[decimal|decimals]] into minutes, and remembering that real journeys speed up and slow down.

st.prompt: A bus travels 90 km at an average speed of 60 km/h. How long does the trip take?
st.reveal: 90 ÷ 60 = 1.5 hours. But 0.5 of an hour is half of 60 minutes, which is 30 minutes. So the trip takes 1 hour 30 minutes. Writing 1.5 as "1 hour 50" is one of the most common mistakes in maths tests.

d.try: Measure a 20-metre stretch in a park or playground with a tape or by counting steps. Time yourself walking it, then running it. Divide 20 by your time in seconds to get your speed in metres per second, then multiply by 3.6 to turn it into km/h.
myth: If you go 30 km/h on the way there and 60 km/h on the way back, your average speed is 45 km/h.
You spend twice as long on the slow half, so it counts for more. For a 60 km trip each way, you take 2 hours there and 1 hour back, covering 120 km in 3 hours. That is 40 km/h.

sec.t:
Say a family drives 90 km to visit their grandparents at an average of 60 km/h. 90 ÷ 60 = 1.5. So the trip takes 1.5 hours.

Here is where many people slip. 1.5 hours is not 1 hour 50 minutes. The .5 means half an hour, and half of 60 minutes is 30. So the answer is 1 hour 30 minutes. In the same way, 0.25 hours is 15 minutes and 0.1 hours is 6 minutes. It is a useful trick to practise with [[@fractions|fractions]].

Units must match too. If the distance is in metres and the speed is in km/h, convert one first. Otherwise the answer is a thousand times wrong.

A car might zoom along at 100 km/h on a highway and then crawl at 10 km/h through a town. What matters for journey time is the average speed for the whole trip. That is total distance divided by total time.

Averages can trick you. Drive 60 km to a town at 30 km/h, which takes 2 hours. Drive back at 60 km/h, which takes 1 hour. You've gone 120 km in 3 hours, so your average is 40 km/h. Most people guess 45. The slow half counts more because you spend longer doing it.

Map apps on phones make these calculations all the time, using live traffic speeds from other phones on the road, as explained in [[@gps-how|how GPS works]].

sec.h: The slow road to the Moon
sec.t:
The Moon is about 384,000 km away. In 1969, Apollo 11 got there in about four days, using a huge rocket that blasted it straight across.

India's [[@chandrayaan|Chandrayaan-3]] launched on 14 July 2023 and landed on 23 August, about 40 days later. That was not because it was slow. ISRO used a smaller rocket, so the spacecraft looped around Earth in bigger and bigger [[orbit|orbits]], picking up speed each time, before swinging out to the Moon. A longer path used far less fuel.

So the shortest trip is not always the best one. And the strangest part? Spacecraft heading to the outer planets often fly past other planets first, stealing a little speed from each. That turns journey-time maths into a puzzle of [[@speed-distance|speed and distance]] across the whole Solar System.

text: Amitabh Bachchan is one of the most famous actors in the history of Indian cinema. Fans call him the Shahenshah, the "emperor". That is partly because of a 1988 film of that name, in which he played a masked avenger, and partly because he ruled Hindi cinema like one for decades.

He became a star in the 1970s playing the "angry young man", a tough outsider fighting injustice. Later he became the friendly host of the quiz show *Kaun Banega Crorepati*, and he is still acting in his eighties. His other nicknames include Big B and Sadi ka Mahanayak, the "superstar of the century".

st.reveal: Films such as Zanjeer and Deewaar cast him as a tough, brooding outsider who takes on smugglers, crooked businessmen and corrupt officials. Writers Salim-Javed created many of these roles, and the "angry young man" label stuck.

d.try: Read a short paragraph from a book aloud in three ways: in your normal voice, in a deep slow voice and in a fast excited voice. Record yourself on a phone with an adult's help. Listen back. Notice how much of an actor's power comes from voice, not just face.
myth: Amitabh Bachchan was an instant success from his first film.
His early films mostly flopped, and some producers thought he was too tall and too thin for a hero. His first big hit, Zanjeer, came in 1973, four years after his debut.

sec.t:
Amitabh was born in 1942 in Allahabad, now Prayagraj. His father, Harivansh Rai Bachchan, was a well-known Hindi poet, best remembered for the long [[@poetry|poem]] *Madhushala*. His mother, Teji Bachchan, was active in theatre. Amitabh sometimes recites his father's verses in public, in the same deep voice audiences know from his films.

After college in Delhi, he worked for a company in Calcutta. According to a story he has often told, he applied to be an announcer at All India Radio and was turned down. That voice would later narrate films and sell everything from paint to chocolate.

sec.h: The accident that stopped a country
sec.t: In 1982, while filming a fight scene for *Coolie* in Bengaluru, Amitabh was hit in the stomach and badly hurt. For weeks his life was in danger. Across India, people prayed in temples, mosques, churches and gurdwaras, and crowds waited outside the hospital in Bombay. When he recovered, the film's makers changed the ending so that his character survived, and froze the frame of the fateful punch on screen.

In 1984 he entered politics and won a seat in Parliament, but he resigned within three years. His film *Shahenshah* came out in 1988 and was a hit. Its dialogue "Rishte mein toh hum tumhare baap lagte hain, naam hai Shahenshah" is still imitated in school playgrounds.

The 1990s were harder. A company he founded ran into heavy debts, and several films failed. Many people thought his career was over.

In 2000, he agreed to host *Kaun Banega Crorepati*, the Indian version of the British show *Who Wants to Be a Millionaire?*. Film stars rarely did television then. The show was a huge hit. His polite, warm manner with contestants from small towns, calling them "devi ji" and "sir", made him a new kind of hero for [[@tv-india|Indian television]].

He went back to films with roles suited to an older actor: fathers, teachers and wise old warriors. In *Kalki 2898 AD* (2024) he played Ashwatthama from the *Mahabharata*. He received the Dadasaheb Phalke Award for 2018, India's highest film honour. More than 50 years after *Zanjeer*, the man once rejected by radio is still one of the busiest voices in Indian entertainment. His films are [[@dubbing-subtitles|dubbed]] into many languages for new audiences.

text: The inside of your nose is lined with thin, damp skin called mucous membrane. Just under it lies a thick web of tiny [[@blood|blood]] vessels. Their job is to warm and wet the air you breathe before it reaches your lungs, so they sit very close to the surface.

That closeness is the problem. When the lining dries out and cracks, gets scratched by a fingernail or takes a knock, a vessel can break. Because the vessels are packed so tightly, even a small break can drip for several minutes.
Most nosebleeds look far worse than they are. A teaspoon of blood spread across a tissue seems like a lot. Almost all nosebleeds stop on their own, or with a few minutes of steady pressure.

st.prompt: Your nose starts bleeding. Where should you press to stop it?

options.t: The soft part of the nose, below the bony bridge
The hard, bony top of the nose

st.reveal: Most nosebleeds start just inside the soft front part of the nose. Pinching there squeezes the broken vessel shut, so a clot can form. Pressing on bone does nothing, because the bone can't squash the vessel.

d.try: Breathe out gently through your nose onto a cold steel spoon or a mirror. The mist that forms is water your nose and airways added to the air. Now breathe the same way on a hot, dry afternoon, or next to a heater, and notice how much drier your nose feels afterwards.
myth: You should tilt your head back to stop a nosebleed.
Leaning back sends blood down the throat, which can make you cough or feel sick. Doctors say to sit up, lean slightly forward and pinch the soft part of the nose.
facts: Little's area (Kiesselbach's area), at the front of the septum
lean forward and pinch the soft part for 10 minutes

sec.t:
Doctors have two names for the trouble spot. The American [[surgeon|surgeon]] James Little described it in 1879, and the German doctor Wilhelm Kiesselbach in 1884, so it is called Little's area or Kiesselbach's area. It sits on the septum, the wall of [[cartilage|cartilage]] that splits your nose into two tunnels, about a fingertip inside. Here, branches of several arteries meet and join up.

About nine out of ten nosebleeds start in this patch. They are called anterior, or front, nosebleeds. They usually come from one nostril and are easy to stop, because you can squeeze the spot from outside.

A much rarer kind starts deep at the back of the nose. These are more common in older adults, can bleed heavily and need a doctor.

Nosebleeds have seasons. In the northern USA they rise in winter, when heaters run all day and indoor air turns dry. In north India, the hot, dusty weeks before the [[@monsoon|monsoon]] do the same, and so can a night spent under a chilly [[@air-conditioning|air conditioner]]. Dry lining cracks like mud at the edge of a pond in May.

Then there's picking. It's the most common cause in children, and doctors are not shy about saying so. A fingernail scrapes the lining, a scab forms, it itches, and it gets picked again. Colds and allergies add to the damage, because sneezing and hard blowing keep the lining sore.

Children between about 2 and 10 get nosebleeds most often. Many simply grow out of them.

{{story:air-conditioning}}

sec.h: What to do when it happens
sec.t:
Sit down and lean slightly forward. Pinch the soft part of your nose, below the bony bridge, firmly with a thumb and finger. Breathe through your mouth and keep pinching for a full 10 minutes by the clock, without letting go to check. Spit out any blood that reaches your mouth.

Many people were taught to tip their head back. That only sends blood down the throat, which can make you cough or feel sick. Lying flat does the same. A cold pack on the bridge of the nose may help a little, but pressure does the real work.

Once it stops, try not to blow your nose or bend over for a few hours, so the fresh clot can hold. The [[@first-aid|first aid]] rules are short enough to learn in a minute.

Most nosebleeds are a nuisance and nothing more. But tell a parent or doctor if one lasts longer than 20 minutes of steady pinching, or follows a hard blow to the head. The same goes for nosebleeds that keep coming back week after week. A doctor can seal a troublesome vessel in a few minutes, a treatment called cautery.

Climbers know nosebleeds well. High up, the air is thin, cold and very dry, and every breath pulls water out of the nose. Trekkers heading to [[@everest-base-camp|Everest Base Camp]], at over 5,000 metres, often carry a small pot of petroleum jelly to dab inside their nostrils. At home, a bowl of water near a heater does a similar job. For most nosebleeds the fix is that simple: keep the lining damp and leave it alone.

text: A chatbot is a computer program you can talk to in ordinary language. Today's best chatbots are built on [[@large-language-models|large language models]], programs that have studied an enormous amount of text: books, websites, articles and more.

From all that reading, the model learns patterns in how words follow each other. When you ask a question, it writes an answer one small chunk at a time, called a token, each time choosing a likely next piece based on everything before it. Because it has seen so many examples, the result can be clear, helpful and surprisingly human-sounding. But it can also be confidently wrong.

st.prompt: A chatbot is asked about a book that does not exist. What might it do?

options.t: Always say it has never heard of the book
Sometimes invent a believable summary and author
Search every library in the world first

st.reveal: Chatbots produce words that fit patterns, so they can make up convincing details. People call this "hallucinating". Newer systems are better at saying "I don't know", but it is always worth checking important facts in a trusted source.

d.try: Play "next word" with friends. One person starts a sentence with one word, and each person adds the single word they think most likely comes next. Then play again choosing surprising words. Notice how the "most likely" story is sensible but dull, and the surprising one goes strange fast.
myth: A chatbot looks up its answers in a giant database of facts.

Most chatbots generate answers from patterns learned in training, not by looking them up. Some are connected to search tools, but the words themselves are still produced one piece at a time, which is why they can sound right and still be wrong.
facts: huge amounts of text, then improved with human feedback

sec.t:
In 1966 Joseph Weizenbaum, a computer scientist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, wrote a program called ELIZA. It pretended to be a therapist. If you typed "I am sad about my mother", it might reply, "Tell me more about your family."

ELIZA understood nothing. It spotted key words and turned your sentences into questions using simple rules. Yet people poured out their feelings to it. Weizenbaum was alarmed by how easily people trusted a machine, and spent much of his later career warning about it.

A model trained only on internet text might repeat rude, false or harmful things it has read. So companies add a second stage. People rate the model's answers, and the model is trained to give the kinds of answers people judged helpful, honest and safe.

This is part of a wider field called [[@ai-safety|AI safety]], which tries to make sure these systems do what people actually want, and refuse requests that could cause harm.

Because a chatbot produces words that sound right, it can sometimes invent facts, quotes or sources that do not exist. People call this hallucinating. It may also give out-of-date information, or reflect unfair ideas found in its training text.

That makes chatbots useful helpers but poor final judges. For homework, health or news, it is wise to check against a trusted book, website or person, the same skills that help you spot [[@fake-news|fake news]].

This is a real argument among scientists. Some say chatbots only shuffle patterns and understand nothing. Others point out that they can solve new problems, explain jokes and write working computer code, and argue that some kind of understanding is happening, even if it is very unlike ours.

[[@alan-turing|Alan Turing]] suggested in 1950 that if a machine could chat so well that you couldn't tell it from a person, we should take its thinking seriously. Modern chatbots can pass short versions of his test, but people still disagree about what that proves.

ChatGPT, released in November 2022, made chatbots famous almost overnight. Today they are built into search engines, phones and school tools, and talking to a computer has become an everyday thing.

text: The Ahom kingdom was founded in 1228 by Sukaphaa, a Tai prince from the hills of what is now northern Myanmar and southern China. He crossed the Patkai hills into the upper [[@brahmaputra|Brahmaputra]] valley and set up his rule there. His [[descendant|descendants]] governed much of today's Assam until 1826, roughly 600 years.

Several things kept them in power. They organised every adult man into a system of shared service, kept careful records, adopted local languages and customs, and used the mighty Brahmaputra river and its forests to defend themselves. They also beat back several large invasions by the [[@mughals|Mughals]].

st.prompt: Under the Ahom paik system, how did most ordinary men pay their dues to the state?

options.t: By working for the kingdom for part of the year
By paying taxes in silver coins
By giving half their rice harvest

st.reveal: Adult men, called paiks, were grouped in teams. Members took turns to serve the state as soldiers or workers, building roads and embankments, while the others kept their farms going. In return each paik got land to farm.

d.try: Try the paik system with friends or family for one week. Divide one daily job, like watering plants or clearing the table, into turns so that each person serves one day while the others rest. At the end, talk about whether sharing the work in turns felt fair.
myth: The Mughals ruled all of India.
Even at their height, the Mughals never conquered several regions, including most of Assam. The Ahoms fought off repeated Mughal campaigns, most famously at Saraighat in 1671.
facts: 1826, when Assam passed to British control

sec.t:
Sukaphaa arrived with a few thousand followers, along with horses and elephants. Rather than trying to wipe out the people already living in the valley, the Ahoms married into local families and brought them into their kingdom.

Over the centuries, the Ahoms came to speak Assamese and many adopted Hinduism, while keeping some of their own Tai customs and [[ritual|rituals]]. The word "Assam" itself is thought by many historians to come from the name Ahom. Rice farming in the flooded valley grew rich, and the kingdom grew with it.

sec.h: Every man a worker and a soldier

sec.t:
The Ahoms kept chronicles called *buranjis*. At first they were written in the Tai Ahom language and script, later in Assamese, on strips of bark from the agar tree. Court officials recorded battles, [[treaty|treaties]], visits from envoys and decisions of the king.

Most Indian kingdoms of the time left [[inscription|inscriptions]] and poems, but few left detailed year-by-year histories. For historians, the buranjis are a treasure.

The Mughals tried many times to conquer Assam. In 1662 the Mughal general Mir Jumla captured the Ahom capital, Garhgaon, but floods, disease and Ahom raids forced his army out.

In 1671, a huge Mughal force led by Raja Ram Singh of Amber came up the Brahmaputra. The Ahom commander Lachit Borphukan met it at Saraighat, near today's Guwahati, where the river narrows between hills. Though seriously ill, Lachit is said to have had himself carried into battle. Small, fast Ahom boats outmanoeuvred the bigger Mughal ships, and the Mughals withdrew. Assam celebrates Lachit Divas every 24 November in his memory.

Ahom kings and queens were buried in moidams, large earth mounds over vaulted chambers, at Charaideo, their first capital. In 2024 the moidams became a [[@unesco-sites|World Heritage Site]], the first cultural site in Northeast India on the list. At Sivasagar, the Rang Ghar, a two-storey pavilion built in the 1700s, let the royal family watch buffalo fights and games at festivals.

In the late 1700s the kingdom was weakened by civil war. Burmese armies invaded several times from 1817. The British drove them out, and under the Treaty of Yandabo in 1826, Assam came under British control. Soon after, they began planting the tea gardens that made [[@assam-tea|Assam tea]] famous worldwide, on land the Ahom paiks once farmed.

text: Enigma was a typewriter-like machine used by Germany's military in the Second World War to scramble messages. Press a key and a different letter lit up. Its spinning wheels moved with each key press, so the code changed with every letter.

Germany believed Enigma could not be broken. But in 1932, Polish mathematicians cracked an early version using clever maths. Just before the war, they shared their secrets with Britain and France. At Bletchley Park in England, thousands of codebreakers, including [[@alan-turing|Alan Turing]], built machines called Bombes to find each day's settings. By the middle of the war, they were reading many German messages, sometimes within hours.

st.prompt: Enigma had one small weakness that helped codebreakers a lot. What was it?

options.t: A letter could never be turned into itself
It always used the same setting on Sundays
It couldn't write the letter Z

st.reveal: Because of how the wiring looped back, an A could become any letter except A. Codebreakers used this to rule out wrong guesses. If they guessed a word was in a message, they knew it couldn't sit where any of its letters matched.

d.try: Make a simple code wheel. Cut two paper circles, one smaller than the other, and write the alphabet around the edge of each. Pin them together at the centre with a split pin so they turn. Turn the inner wheel three letters and use it to send a friend a secret message.
myth: Alan Turing built the first computer to crack Enigma.

Turing designed the Bombe, an electrical machine with spinning drums that tested Enigma settings. It was not a computer. The Colossus computers at Bletchley Park, built by engineer Tommy Flowers, attacked a different German code called Lorenz.

sec.h: A machine with billions of choices
sec.t:
An Enigma looked like a typewriter in a wooden box. Inside were three [[rotor|rotors]], wheels with 26 contacts on each side, wired in a jumbled way. When you pressed a key, electricity ran through the rotors and lit up a different letter. Then the first rotor clicked forward one step, changing the whole path.

At the front was a plugboard that swapped pairs of letters, adding even more mixing. With all the choices of rotors, starting positions and plugs, an army Enigma had about 159 quintillion possible settings. Checking them one by one, even at one per second, would take far longer than the age of the universe.

Bletchley Park was a country house north of London. By 1945, about 10,000 people worked there, around three-quarters of them women. They included mathematicians, chess players, crossword fans and linguists. Some were recruited after solving a newspaper crossword quickly.

Turing and Gordon Welchman designed the British Bombe, a cupboard-sized machine with rows of spinning drums. Codebreakers fed it a guessed word, called a crib. German messages often contained predictable phrases, such as weather reports. The Bombe raced through settings that could match, and threw out impossible ones. Each day, the team then tested the survivors by hand. Many staff were in their late teens or early twenties, working in wooden huts in shifts round the clock.

Enigma's design had a flaw: no letter could ever become itself. Lazy operators made it worse by using easy starting positions, like ABC, or repeating the same phrases daily.

Navies helped too. In May 1941, British sailors boarded a sinking German submarine, U-110, and grabbed its codebooks and settings sheets. The German navy later added a fourth rotor, which locked out Bletchley for most of 1942 until new captures and faster Bombes helped them catch up.

Information from Enigma, code-named Ultra, helped the Allies find submarines in the Atlantic and plan for D-Day in 1944. Some historians think it shortened the [[@world-war-two|Second World War]] by two years or more, though others think the effect is hard to measure.

After the war, everyone was sworn to secrecy. Many codebreakers never told their families. The story came out only in the 1970s. And the strangest part? A different code-breaking project at Bletchley led to Colossus, one of the world's [[@first-computers|first computers]], and today every phone uses far stronger [[@encryption|encryption]] than Enigma ever had.

text: India's first newspaper was *Hicky's Bengal Gazette*, first printed in Calcutta on 29 January 1780. Its founder, James Augustus Hicky, was an Irishman who had come to India and fallen into debt. While in prison for that debt, he learned about printing, and when he got out he started a weekly paper.

It was only two sheets, printed on both sides, and full of gossip, adverts, poems and news from ships. But it also mocked the most powerful people in British India, including the Governor-General, Warren Hastings. Within two years, the authorities shut it down.

st.prompt: How did the government finally stop Hicky's newspaper in 1782?

options.t: It seized his printing press and type
It bought every copy before it could be sold

st.reveal: After a string of court cases, officials sent men to take away Hicky's press and metal type. Without them he couldn't print a single page, and India's first newspaper fell silent.

d.try: Make a one-page family newspaper. Give it a name, a date and a headline about something real that happened at home this week. Add a weather report, a "notices" box and a drawing. Hicky wrote most of his paper himself too.
myth: The first newspapers in India were started by Indians fighting for freedom.
The very first was started by an Irishman, James Augustus Hicky, in 1780. Indian-owned papers in Indian languages came a few decades later, and many of them did go on to fight for freedom.

sec.t:
Calcutta in 1780 was the capital of the [[@east-india-company|East India Company]]'s [[territory|territory]]. Company officials made fortunes, sometimes dishonestly, and nobody dared to write about it. Hicky did. He gave them nicknames, hinted at bribes and complained about how ordinary soldiers and poor Calcuttans were treated.

The paper was hugely popular. People passed copies around and read them aloud in taverns and coffee houses. Hicky called his paper "open to all parties, but influenced by none".

Rich officials were not the only targets. Hicky also wrote about leaking roofs, rubbish in the streets, dangerous horse carriages and the hardships of poor European soldiers. His paper carried adverts for runaway servants, ships leaving for England, wine, horses and lost property, which today give historians a rare look at daily life in 18th-century Calcutta.

Other English papers followed in Calcutta, Madras and Bombay. Indian-language papers came next. In 1818, missionaries at Serampore, near Calcutta, began *Samachar Darpan* in Bengali. In 1822, Fardunji Marzban started *Bombay Samachar* in Gujarati, and it is still published today.

Reformer [[@raja-ram-mohan-roy|Raja Ram Mohan Roy]] started papers in Bengali and Persian in the early 1820s to argue for social change and against practices he thought were cruel. On 30 May 1826, *Udant Martand*, the first Hindi newspaper, appeared in Calcutta. It lasted only about a year and a half, but 30 May is still marked as Hindi Journalism Day. It closed partly because sending copies by post to Hindi readers far away cost too much.

As the freedom movement grew, newspapers became one of its sharpest tools. Bal Gangadhar Tilak ran *Kesari* in Marathi and was jailed for what he wrote. Mahatma Gandhi edited *Young India* and *Harijan*. The British passed laws to control the press, and editors were often fined or imprisoned.

The *Times of India* began in 1838 as *The Bombay Times and Journal of Commerce*. *The Hindu* started in Madras in 1878, set up by a group of young men who were angry about how the British-run papers treated Indians.

India today has one of the biggest newspaper markets on Earth. Crores of copies roll off presses every night in dozens of languages, and Hindi papers such as *Dainik Jagran* and *Dainik Bhaskar* are among the most-read in the world. Much of their news is now read on phones too. Yet every story still starts the same way it did in Hicky's day, with someone asking questions, which is the heart of [[@journalism|journalism]].

text: The Quit India Movement was a mass campaign launched by Mahatma [[@gandhi|Gandhi]] and the Indian National Congress in August 1942, during the Second World War. It demanded that the British leave India immediately.

On 8 August 1942, at a meeting in Bombay, Gandhi told Indians to "do or die": to act as if they were already free. Within hours, the British arrested almost every Congress leader. Leaderless, people across India protested anyway, with strikes, marches and in some places attacks on railways and government buildings. The government crushed the movement within months and arrested more than 100,000 people. But it showed that Britain could no longer count on Indian cooperation.

st.prompt: After Gandhi and other leaders were arrested, who raised the Congress flag at the Bombay meeting ground on 9 August 1942?

options.t: Aruna Asaf Ali, a young Congress member
Gandhi himself, before the police arrived

st.reveal: With the senior leaders in jail, Aruna Asaf Ali hoisted the flag at Gowalia Tank Maidan. She then went into hiding and helped lead the underground movement. The ground is now called August Kranti Maidan.

src: Bipan Chandra and others, India's Struggle for Independence (Penguin, 1988).
Encyclopaedia Britannica, Quit India Movement.
Sumit Sarkar, Modern India 1885–1947 (Macmillan, 1983).
n.certNote: Historians agree on what happened in 1942. They disagree about how much the movement achieved. Some see it as the final push that convinced Britain to leave; others argue that the war, money troubles in Britain and later events mattered more.

myth: The Quit India Movement was entirely peaceful.

Gandhi asked for non-violent action, but with the leaders in jail, the movement had no central control. Some protesters cut telegraph wires, damaged railway lines and attacked police stations, and the government used heavy force in return.

sec.t:
The [[@world-war-two|Second World War]] had reached India's doorstep. Japan had conquered Burma and was near the eastern border. Britain had declared India part of the war in 1939 without asking Indian leaders.

In early 1942, the British sent Sir Stafford Cripps to offer India self-government, but only after the war. Congress leaders rejected the offer. Gandhi is said to have called it "a post-dated cheque". He argued that only a free India could defend itself properly, and that the British should leave now.

With the leaders gone, younger people stepped forward. Aruna Asaf Ali raised the Congress flag at Gowalia Tank on 9 August, then went into hiding. Jayaprakash Narayan and Ram Manohar Lohia organised resistance in secret.

Usha Mehta and a few others ran the Congress Radio, a secret station that moved from place to place in Bombay to avoid detection. It broadcast news the censored newspapers would not print, until the police found it in November 1942. In a few places, such as Ballia in Uttar Pradesh, Satara in Maharashtra and Tamluk in Bengal, local people set up their own governments for weeks or even years.

The government struck back hard. Police and troops fired on crowds, and many protesters were killed, including Matangini Hazra, a 73-year-old woman shot while leading a march in Tamluk. Whole villages were fined.

Not all Indians joined in. The Muslim League stayed away, as did the Communist Party, which supported the war against Nazi Germany after it invaded the Soviet Union. Many Indians were serving in the army. Meanwhile, [[@subhas-bose|Subhas Chandra Bose]] chose a different path, raising an army with Japanese help.

By early 1943 the open protests had been crushed. Gandhi was released in 1944 because of poor health. Yet the movement made clear that millions of Indians wanted freedom and were willing to suffer for it.

After the war, Britain was exhausted and short of money. Historians still argue over how far Quit India forced its hand. Five years after "do or die", on 15 August 1947, India became independent. The Bombay ground where it began is now called August Kranti Maidan, the August Revolution Ground.

text: China is huge. It covers about 9.6 million km², about three times the size of India and close to the size of the USA. Only Russia and Canada are clearly bigger, and China and the USA are so close in size that the ranking depends on how you count water and disputed land.
China also has an enormous population, about 1.4 billion people. For a long time it had more people than any other country. In 2023, the United Nations estimated that India had overtaken it.

st.prompt: China stretches about 5,000 km from east to west. How many time zones does it officially use?
st.reveal: The whole country runs on Beijing time. In the far west, in Xinjiang, the Sun can rise as late as 9 or 10 in the morning by the clock. Many people there also use an unofficial local time two hours behind.

myth: The Great Wall of China is the only human-made object you can see from space, even from the Moon.

From the Moon no human-made objects can be seen with the naked eye. From low orbit, the wall is very hard to spot because it is narrow and similar in colour to the land. China's first astronaut, Yang Liwei, said he could not see it.

sec.t:
China's land steps down from west to east, like a giant staircase. In the south-west is the Tibetan Plateau, so high that it is called the roof of the world. [[@everest-first|Mount Everest]] sits on the border with [[@nepal|Nepal]]. In the north-west lie the Taklamakan and Gobi deserts.

Two great rivers flow east across the country. The Yangtze, about 6,300 km long, is the longest river in Asia. The Yellow River gets its name from the yellow silt it carries. Most people live in the flatter, wetter east, where cities such as Shanghai and [[@beijing|Beijing]] hold more than 2 crore people each.

China stretches across about 5,000 km, which would naturally cover five time zones. But since 1949, the whole country has used Beijing time. In the east, the Sun rises at a normal hour. In the far west, in Xinjiang, the Sun can rise after 9 am in winter, and people adjust their working hours.

India, which is smaller, also uses one time zone. The USA, by contrast, uses several [[@time-zones|time zones]] across the mainland.

The Great Wall is not one wall but many walls built over about 2,000 years by different [[dynasty|dynasties]] to protect against raids from the north. A survey published in 2012 found all its sections together run about 21,000 km. Much of what visitors see today was built during the Ming dynasty, 1368 to 1644.

Since 2008, China has built more high-speed railway than all other countries put together, over 40,000 km of track. [[@bullet-trains|Bullet trains]] link most large cities, running at up to about 350 km/h.

Every year around the Chinese [[@new-year|New Year]], also called the Spring Festival, hundreds of millions of people travel home to their families. Officials count several billion journeys over about 40 days, making it the largest yearly movement of people on Earth.

China is home to the giant panda, which lives in mountain [[@bamboo|bamboo]] forests in the south-west. Thanks to protection, its numbers have risen, and it is no longer listed as [[endangered|endangered]].

[[@chinese-characters|Mandarin]] Chinese is spoken by more people as a first language than any other language. China also has many other languages and [[dialect|dialects]], such as Cantonese, as well as 56 officially recognised ethnic groups.

text: A living root bridge is a bridge grown from the roots of a living tree. In the hills of Meghalaya, in north-east India, Khasi and Jaintia villagers plant rubber fig trees on riverbanks. These trees send out [[aerial-root|aerial roots]], roots that grow from the trunk and branches into the air.

Builders guide those roots across a stream, along a frame of bamboo or hollow palm trunks. When the roots reach the other side, they dig into the soil. Over years, they thicken and grow into one another, forming a living, walkable bridge. Stones are pushed into the gaps to make a path. Some bridges can carry dozens of people at once.

st.prompt: How do villagers get the fig roots to grow across a river in the right direction?

options.t: They guide them along hollow tree trunks or bamboo frames
They pull them across with ropes every morning
They let the roots float on the water until they reach the other bank

st.reveal: Builders lay split areca palm trunks or bamboo across the stream, and train the young aerial roots along them. Once the roots reach the far bank, they grow into the soil, thicken and slowly take the weight.

src: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Tentative List, Jingkieng Jri, Living Root Bridge Cultural Landscapes.
Government of Meghalaya, Department of Tourism.
n.certNote: The bridges are real and well studied. Their ages are hard to measure, so claims that some are several hundred years old are estimates passed down by villagers, not proven dates.
